en: Dīgha Nikāya 14: Mahāpadāna Sutta 1. Discourse on the Recollection of Past Lives The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in the mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Lord; it is marvelous, Lord! How well-spoken by the Blessed One were these words: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Yet, Lord, I do not see even one other thing by which, when it is developed and cultivated, the unarisen taints do not arise, and the arisen taints are abandoned, as much as this very mindfulness of the body. For mindfulness of the body, Lord, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints. "It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda! Mindfulness of the body, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints.

And how, Ānanda, is mindfulness of the body developed and cultivated so that the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally... He dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mind in the mind internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. In this way, Ānanda, mindfulness of the body is developed and cultivated so that the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take a blade of grass, a stalk of reed, or a piece of wood, and at the end of each day he were to deposit it in a heap, saying: ‘This is my mother, this is my mother’s mother,’ and were to continue in this way for a hundred years, he would not reach the end of his mothers’ lineage, nor would the heap of grass, reeds, or wood come to an end. So vast, bhikkhus, is the round of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). Its beginning is not known, obscured by ignorance and fettered by craving. For such a long time, you have undergone suffering, experienced pain, and endured distress. Enough, bhikkhus, of heaping up more fuel for this suffering. Now, with the complete destruction of the taints, you must dwell in the state of final knowledge (*aññā*) and attain *parinibbāna*. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was seated near the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Lord, it is wonderful, Lord; it is marvelous, Lord! How well-spoken by the Blessed One were these words: ‘So vast, bhikkhus, is the round of rebirth. Its beginning is not known... Yet, Lord, I do not see even one other thing by which, when it is developed and cultivated, the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned, as much as this very mindfulness of the body. For mindfulness of the body, Lord, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints. "It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda! Mindfulness of the body, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints. And how, Ānanda, is mindfulness of the body developed and cultivated so that the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally... He dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mind in the mind internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally... externally... both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. In this way, Ānanda, mindfulness of the body is developed and cultivated so that the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Another person is a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*); having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering. Another person is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*); having passed away from here, he will attain final *nibbāna* in the higher realms without returning from that world. Another person is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was seated near the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Lord, it is wonderful, Lord; it is marvelous, Lord! How well-spoken by the Blessed One were these words: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Yet, Lord, I do not see even one other thing by which, when it is developed and cultivated, the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned, as much as this very mindfulness of the body. For mindfulness of the body, Lord, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints. "It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda! Mindfulness of the body, Ānanda, when developed and cultivated, leads to the non-arising of the unarisen taints and to the abandoning of the arisen taints. And how, Ānanda, is mindfulness of the body developed and cultivated so that the unarisen taints do not arise and the arisen taints are abandoned? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful,
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, in the Kareri hut.

Then, after the meal, on their return from almsround, a large number of bhikkhus gathered and sat together in the Kareri pavilion, and a discussion concerning past lives arose among them as they were seated there.
“Such was my former dwelling, such was my former dwelling.
With his divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One heard this conversation between those bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One rose from his seat, went to the Kareri pavilion, and having arrived, sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation that was left unfinished?
When this was said, those monks replied to the Blessed One:

“Here, Bhante, after we had returned from our almsround following the meal, we were sitting together and assembled in the Kareri pavilion when a talk on the Dhamma concerning past lives arose among us.”
‘Such was my former dwelling, such was my former dwelling.
This, Bhante, was our conversation that remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.
“Bhikkhus, would you like to hear a Dhamma talk concerning past lives?”
“Bhagavā, this is the time;
Sugata, this is the time for the Bhagavā to deliver a Dhamma discourse concerning past lives. Having heard it from the Bhagavā, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, ninety-one aeons ago from now, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.”
In this very same thirty-first aeon, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
In that same thirty-first aeon, monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
In this very same auspicious aeon, monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
In this very auspicious aeon, monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
In this very auspicious aeon, monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
In this very auspicious aeon, monks, I myself have now appeared in the world as the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a khattiya; he arose in a khattiya family.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a khattiya; he arose in a khattiya family.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a khattiya; he arose in a khattiya family.”
"Monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a brahmin; he arose in a brahmin family.
Monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a brahmin; he arose in a brahmin family.
Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was by birth a brahmin; he arose in a brahmin family."
“Monks, at present I am an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, a kshatriya by birth, born into a kshatriya clan.
Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña lineage.
Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña lineage.”
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Kassapa clan.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Kassapa clan.”
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Kassapa clan.
Bhikkhus, I, at present, am the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and am of the Gotama clan.
Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years.”
Monks, the lifespan of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī was seventy thousand years.
Monks, the lifespan of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vessabhū was sixty thousand years.
Monks, the lifespan of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha was forty thousand years.
“Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was thirty thousand years.
Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was twenty thousand years.
Bhikkhus, my lifespan at present is short, limited, and brief; whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.”
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a pāṭali tree.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a puṇḍarīka tree.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a sāla tree.”
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a sirīsa tree.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of an udumbara tree.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a nigrodha tree.”
“Monks, I am now the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, awakened at the foot of an Assattha tree.
Monks, the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One Vipassī had a pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa, a most excellent pair.
Monks, the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One Sikhī had a pair of chief disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava, a most excellent pair.”
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vessabhu had a pair of chief disciples named Soṇa and Uttara, a most auspicious pair.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha had a pair of chief disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, a most auspicious pair.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Koṇāgamana had a pair of chief disciples named Bhiyyosa and Uttara, a most auspicious pair.
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja, a noble pair.
Bhikkhus, now, in my time, I have a pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna, a noble pair.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had three assemblies of disciples.”
There were three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus;
one assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand bhikkhus; and one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus.
These, monks, were the three assemblies of disciples of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Vipassi.
[This] was true for all those whose taints were exhausted.
Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had three assemblies of disciples.
One assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand monks; another assembly of disciples...
There were eighty thousand bhikkhus; there was one assembly of disciples consisting of seventy thousand bhikkhus.
Bhikkhus, these were the three assemblies of disciples that occurred for the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—all of whom were indeed those whose taints were exhausted.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One Vessabhu, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there were three assemblies of disciples.
One assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus; one assembly of disciples consisted of seventy thousand bhikkhus;
and one assembly of disciples consisted of sixty thousand bhikkhus.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vessabhū, there were these three assemblies of disciples,
all of whom were destroyers of the taints.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha, there was one assembly of disciples.
There were forty thousand bhikkhus. Bhikkhus, this was the one assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, all of whom had destroyed the taints.
Bhikkhus, there was one assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One... [all of whom had destroyed the taints].
There were thirty thousand bhikkhus. Bhikkhus, this was the one assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, all of whom had destroyed the taints.
Bhikkhus, there was one assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One...
There were twenty thousand bhikkhus. Monks, this was the one assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
all of them were indeed those whose taints were destroyed.

Monks, at present, there has been one assembly of my disciples consisting of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. Monks, this is the one assembly of my disciples; all of them are indeed those whose taints are destroyed.
“Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a monk named Asoka as his attendant, his chief attendant.
Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a monk named Khemaṅkara as his attendant, his chief attendant.
Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a monk named Upasanta as his attendant, his chief attendant.”
“Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha, the bhikkhu named Buddhija was his attendant, his chief attendant.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Koṇāgamana, the bhikkhu named Sotthija was his attendant, his chief attendant.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, the bhikkhu named Sabbamitta was his attendant, his chief attendant.”
“Bhikkhus, at present Ānanda is my attendant, my chief attendant.
Bhikkhus, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī, there was a king named Bandhumā who was his father;
and there was a queen named Bandhumatī who was his mother.”
King Bandhuma’s royal capital was the city named Bandhumatī.
Monks, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī had a father named King Aruṇa,
and his mother, the queen who gave birth to him, was named Pabhāvatī.
The capital city of King Aruṇa was named Aruṇavatī.
Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhu, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a father named King Suppatiṭṭha and a mother,
the queen-consort, named Vassavatī.
The royal capital of King Suppatiṭṭha was the city named Anoma.
Bhikkhus, the brahmin Aggidatta was the father of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
the brahmin woman Visākhā was his mother, who gave him birth.
Now at that time, monks, there was a king named Khema.
King Khema’s capital city was named Khemavatī.
And for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Koṇāgamana, there was a brahmin father named Yaññadatta.
The mother who gave birth was a brahmin woman named Uttarā.
At that time, monks, there was a king named Sobha.
King Sobha’s royal capital was a city named Sobhavatī.
Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a brahmin father named Brahmadatta and a brahmin mother,
his progenitress, named Dhanavatī.
At that time, monks, there was a king named Kikī.
For King Kiki, the capital city was named Bārāṇasī.
For me, monks, at the present time, there was a king named Suddhodana as my father;
a queen named Māyā was my mother, who gave birth to me.
“The city named Kapilavatthu was the royal capital.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this discussion arose among those bhikkhus:

"It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends! Such is the great psychic power and great majesty of the Tathāgata, in that the Tathāgata [remembers] the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, whose proliferations are cut off, whose round of existence is severed, and whose cycle is exhausted."

Having transcended all suffering, he will also recollect [his past lives] by way of birth, he will recollect them by way of name, he will recollect them by way of clan, he will recollect them by way of the measure of their lifespan, he will recollect them by way of their pairs of disciples, and he will recollect them by way of their assemblies of disciples:

"Those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a birth; those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, of such-and-such virtue, of such-and-such Dhamma, of such-and-such wisdom, of such-and-such a mode of dwelling, and of such-and-such a liberation."
“Friends, is it only the Tathāgata who has thoroughly penetrated this Dhamma-element,
by whose thorough penetration of the Dhamma-element the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferations are cut off,
the course is finished, the round is ended, and who have transcended all suffering— recollecting them by their birth, by their names, and by their clans?”
He recollects even the measure of their lifespans; he recollects even their pairs of disciples; he recollects even their assemblies of disciples:
"Those Blessed Ones were of such birth, and they were thus named, thus surnamed, of such virtue, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such a way of dwelling, and thus liberated."
Or did deities inform the Tathāgata of this matter, by which the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna,
for whom the proliferations have been cut off, the pathways of rebirth have been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering—
recollecting them by their birth, by their names, by their clans, by the measure of their lifespans, and even by their pairs of chief disciples?
He recollects them; he even recollects the assemblies of disciples:
“Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, they were of such names, such clans, such conduct, such doctrines, such wisdom, such dwellings, and such liberations,” so he recollects them.
And this conversation among those bhikkhus remained unfinished.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Kareri pavilion; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you gathered here now? And what was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished?"
When this was said, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this discussion arose among us:
‘It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends! How great is the Tathāgata’s power and majesty!’”
For it is indeed remarkable that the Tathāgata, regarding the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of existence has been cut off,
the cycle of rebirth has been severed, the round of becoming has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering— remembers them by their birth, remembers them by their names,
remembers them by their clans, remembers them by the measure of their lifespans, remembers them by their pairs of chief disciples, and remembers them by their assemblies of disciples.
“‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth,’ and ‘those Blessed Ones were of such a name, such a clan, such virtue, such a doctrine, such wisdom,
such a dwelling, and such a liberation’— is this, friend, the very element of Dhamma (dhammadhātu) thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata alone,

through the thorough penetration of which the Tathāgata [knows] the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, whose proliferations are cut off, whose round of existence is severed, and whose cycle is brought to an end?”

Having transcended all suffering, he recollects [his past lives] even by way of birth, he recollects them even by way of name, he recollects them even by way of clan, he recollects them even by way of the measure of his lifespan, he recollects them even by way of pairs of disciples, and he recollects them even by way of assemblies of disciples:

“Those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a birth; those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, of such-and-such virtue, of such-and-such Dhamma, of such-and-such wisdom, of such-and-such a dwelling, and of such-and-such liberation.”
Or did deities inform the Tathāgata of this matter, whereby the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna—
whose proliferations are cut off, whose pathways are severed, whose cycle is ended, and who have transcended all suffering— and who recollect them by their birth,
by their names, by their clans, by the measure of their lifespans, and by their pairs of disciples?
“He recollects them, and he also recollects the assemblies of disciples:
‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth; they were of such names, such clans, such conduct, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such dwellings, and such liberation.
This was our conversation, Bhante, which remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.”
“Monks, this very Dhamma-element has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata; because of his thorough penetration of this Dhamma-element,

the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferations are cut off, the cycle is ended, the round is finished, and who have transcended all suffering—
he recollects them by their birth, he recollects them by their names, he recollects them by their clans, and he recollects them by the measure of their lifespans.”
He recollects even the pairs of disciples, and he recollects even the assemblies of disciples:
"Those Blessed Ones were of such birth; they were of such names, such clans, such conduct, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such dwellings, and such liberation.
Deities also informed the Tathāgata of this matter concerning the Buddhas of the past who had attained final Nibbāna.
Having cut off proliferation, having cut off the tether, having exhausted the cycle, and having transcended all suffering, he recollects his past births,
recollects his names, recollects his clans, recollects the measure of his lifespan, recollects the pairs of disciples,
and recollects the assemblies of disciples:

‘Those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a birth,’ and ‘those Blessed Ones were of such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a virtue, such-and-such a doctrine, such-and-such wisdom, such-and-such a dwelling, and such-and-such a liberation.
Would you like to hear, monks, a further Dhamma talk concerning past lives?
“This is the time for it, Blessed One; this is the time for it, Sugata.”
“If the Blessed One would give a further discourse on the Dhamma connected with past lives, the bhikkhus, having heard it from the Blessed One, will remember it.
“Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely; I shall speak,” [the Blessed One said].
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"Monks, ninety-one aeons ago from now, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of khattiya birth; he appeared in a khattiya family."
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan.
Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Pāṭali tree.”
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa, a most auspicious pair.
Bhikkhus, there were three assemblies of disciples for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

One assembly of disciples consisted of sixty-eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; one assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand bhikkhus; and one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had these three assemblies of disciples, all of whom were destroyers of the taints.
Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a monk named Asoka as his chief attendant.
Bhikkhus, King Bandhumā was the father of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The queen named Bandhumatī was his mother, his progenitress.
For King Bandhuma, there was a city named Bandhumatī which served as his royal capital.
2. The Dhamma-nature of the Bodhisatta.
Then, monks, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, passing away from the Tusita realm, descended into his mother’s womb mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is the natural law here.
It is the natural law, monks, that when the Bodhisatta passes away from the Tusita realm and descends into his mother’s womb, this occurs.
Then, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, a measureless and sublime radiance appeared,
surpassing even the splendor of the gods. Even in those intermediate spaces between worlds— which are gloomy, obscure, and shrouded in blinding darkness,
where even these moons and suns, so powerful and majestic, do not reach with their light— there too a measureless and sublime radiance appeared.
An immeasurable and sublime radiance appears in the world, surpassing even the splendor of the devas.
Even those beings who have been reborn there recognize one another by that light, saying: "It seems, friends, that other beings too have been reborn here.
And this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, quakes, and shakes violently. An immeasurable and sublime radiance appears in the world, surpassing even the splendor of the devas.
This is the natural law in this regard.
This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, four sons of the gods approach from the four quarters for his protection, [thinking]: "Let no human..."
‘or a non-human being, or anyone at all, will cause him harm.
This is the natural law in this regard.
It is the natural law, monks, that when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, she is by nature virtuous and observant of her vows.

She is the mother of a bodhisattva; she abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness.
This is the natural law in this regard.
It is the natural law, monks, that when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb,
no thought associated with the strands of sensual pleasure arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother toward men, and the Bodhisatta’s mother cannot be overcome by any man with a lustful mind.
This is the natural law in this regard.

This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, the Bodhisatta’s mother becomes a recipient of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Endowed with and possessed of these five strands of sensual pleasure, she enjoys herself.
This is the natural law in this regard.
This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, no affliction whatsoever arises for the Bodhisatta’s mother.
The Bodhisatta’s mother is happy and her body is free from fatigue;
and the Bodhisatta’s mother sees the Bodhisatta within her womb, complete in all limbs and faculties, with no organ lacking.
“Monks, suppose there were a beautiful beryl gem of pure birth, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear,
translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every respect. Into it was strung a thread— blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale yellow.”
A man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it:
"This is indeed a beautiful beryl gem, of noble birth, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every way.
Herein, this thread is strung through it—blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale yellow."
In the same way, monks, when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, no affliction whatsoever arises for the Bodhisatta’s mother;
the Bodhisatta’s mother is happy and her body is free from fatigue.
And the Bodhisatta’s mother sees the Bodhisatta within her womb, complete in all limbs and faculties, with no organ lacking.
This is the natural law in this case.
This is the natural law, monks: when seven days have passed since the birth of the Bodhisatta, the mother of the Bodhisatta passes away and is reborn in the Tusita realm.
This is the natural law in this case.
This is the natural law, monks: whereas other women give birth after carrying the fetus in their womb for nine or ten months, the mother of a Bodhisatta does not give birth in this way.
For exactly ten months the mother of a Bodhisatta carries the Bodhisatta in her womb before she gives birth.
This is the natural law here.

This is the natural law, monks: whereas other women give birth while sitting or lying down, the mother of a Bodhisatta does not give birth in such a way; rather, the mother of a Bodhisatta gives birth while standing.
This is the natural law here.
This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, the devas receive him first, and afterwards human beings.
This is the natural law in this regard.
This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, before the Bodhisatta has even reached the ground...
He becomes earth; four sons of gods receive him and place him before his mother, saying:
"Be joyful, O Queen! A son of great power has been born to you.
This is the natural law in this regard.

This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges quite clean, unsullied by water, unsullied by mucus, unsullied by blood, unsullied by any impurity—pure and clean.
Just as, monks, a precious gem placed upon a Kāsī cloth does not soil the Kāsī cloth, nor does the Kāsī cloth soil the precious gem. And why is that?
Because both are pure.

In the same way, monks, when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges quite clean, unsullied—unsullied by water, unsullied by mucus, unsullied by blood, pure and clean, untainted by anything impure.
This is the natural law in this regard.

This is the natural law, monks: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, two streams of water appear from the sky—one cool and one warm—with which they perform the water-rites for the Bodhisatta and for the mother.
This is the natural law in this regard.
This is the natural law, monks: immediately after birth, the Bodhisatta, having stood with level feet, proceeds seven steps facing north while a white parasol is held over him;
he surveys all the directions and utters this lion’s roar:
“I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world.”
‘This is the last birth for the world; now there is no further becoming.
This is the natural law in this regard.
It is the natural law, monks, that when the Bodhisatta issues from his mother’s womb, then, together with the world of devas...
In the world with its Māras and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, a measureless and sublime radiance appears,
surpassing even the splendor of the devas.
Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, unsheltered, and shrouded in blinding darkness where even these suns and moons [do not reach]— are illuminated.
Though they possess such great psychic power and such great majesty, they do not outshine [the radiance] with their own light;
rather, there too a measureless, sublime effulgence appears, surpassing even the divine power of the gods.
And those beings who have been reborn there recognize one another by that light, saying: "It seems, friends, that there are other beings also reborn here."
And this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes, and quakes; and an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears in the world, surpassing even the splendor of the devas.
This is the natural law in this regard.
3. The Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man.
When Prince Vipassī was born, monks, they reported to King Bandhuma:
“A son has been born to you, Your Majesty; let Your Majesty behold him.
King Bandhuma beheld Prince Vipassī, and having seen him, he summoned the brahmin soothsayers and said this to them:
"Let the honorable fortune-telling brahmins behold the prince.
The fortune-telling brahmins, monks, beheld Prince Vipassī; having seen him, they said this to King Bandhumant:
"Be joyful, O Lord! A son of great power has been born to you. It is a gain for you, Great King; it is a great blessing for you, Great King, that such a son as this has been born into your family."
For this prince, O King, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, for whom there are only two possible destinies and no other.

If he dwells in the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, established in stability throughout the land, and possessed of the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures:
That is to say: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without punishment or sword, through righteousness alone, he dwells therein.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, with the veil lifted from the world.
And by what thirty-two marks of a Great Man, O King, is this prince endowed, such that for a Great Man possessing them there are only two possible destinies and no other?

If he dwells at home, he becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in the land and is possessed of the seven treasures.
For him, these seven treasures come into being:
namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Thus he dwells having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean, without rod or sword, but by righteousness.
And if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, with the veil lifted in the world.
For this prince, O King, has well-placed feet. Because this prince, O King, has well-placed feet...
This too is a mark of a Great Man belonging to this Great Man.

Your Majesty, on the soles of this prince's feet, wheels have appeared, with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs, perfect in every respect. That these wheels have appeared on the soles of this prince's feet...
They have a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in every respect; this too is a mark of a Great Man belonging to this Great Man.
For this Prince, O King, has long heels...
[and so on] ...For this Prince, O King, has long fingers... [and so on].
For this prince, O King, has soft and delicate hands and feet...
[as before] ...for this prince, O King, has webbed hands and feet...
[as before] ...for this prince, O King, has high-arched feet... [as before].
For this prince, O King, has legs like those of an antelope...
For this prince, O King, while standing and without bending, can touch and rub both knees with the palms of his hands...
For this prince, O King, has the private parts enclosed in a sheath...
For this prince, O King, is golden-hued, with skin like refined gold...
For this prince, O King, has delicate skin; because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body...
For this prince, O King, has single hairs growing from each pore; the hairs grow one by one from each hair-follicle...
For this prince, O King, has upward-pointing body hair; his hairs grow pointing upwards, blue in color like the hue of collyrium, curled, and turned to the right...
[as before] ...For this prince, O King, has a body straight as Brahmā’s;...
[as before] ...For this prince, O King, has seven protuberances;... [as before] ...
For this prince, O King, has the forequarters of a lion...
[as before] ...For this prince, O King, has a girth between his shoulders...
[as before] ...For this prince, O King, is well-proportioned like a banyan tree: as tall as he is, so wide is his span; as wide as his span, so tall is he... [as before].
For this prince, O King, has a symmetrical trunk... [and so on]...
For this prince, O King, has the excellence of the supreme sense of taste... [and so on]...
For this prince, O King, has a jaw like that of a lion... [and so on].
For this prince, O King, has forty teeth … [as before] … For this prince,
O King, has even teeth … [as before] … For this prince,
O King, has teeth without gaps … [as before].
For this prince, O King, has very white teeth...
For this prince, O King, has a long tongue...
For this prince, O King, has a Brahma-voice like the song of the karavīka bird...
For this prince, O King, has deep blue eyes ... [as before] ...
For this prince, O King, has eyelashes like those of a cow ...
[as before] ... On the space between his eyebrows, O King, this prince has a tuft of hair that is white, soft as cotton. Also, this—
"Your Majesty, between the eyebrows of the prince there is a tuft of hair, white and soft like cotton;
this too is a mark of a Great Man for this Great Man.
Furthermore, Your Majesty, this prince has a cranial protuberance on his head; that too is a mark of a Great Man for this Great Man."
"Your Majesty, this prince is endowed with these thirty-two marks of a Great Man, for which there are only two possible destinies for a Great Man and no other.

If he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch—righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has attained stability in his realm and is possessed of the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures."
That is to say: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean, without the rod and without the sword, through righteousness, he dwells therein.
‘But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he will become an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, one who has drawn aside the veil in the world.
Then, monks, King Bandhuma had the Brahmins skilled in signs clothed in unwashed garments and satisfied them with all their desires.
Then, monks, King Bandhuma appointed nurses for Prince Vipassī.
Some suckled him, some bathed him, some carried him, and others bore him on their hips.
And from the moment Prince Vipassī was born, monks, a white parasol was held over him both by day and by night:
‘May cold or heat, grass, dust, or dew not afflict him.
And once born, monks, Prince Vipassī was dear and pleasing to many people—
just as, monks, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus is dear and pleasing to many people.
In the same way, monks, Prince Vipassī was dear and pleasing to many people;
he was carried from lap to lap.
And when Prince Vipassī was born, monks, he possessed a sweet voice, a melodious voice, a pleasant voice, and a charming voice.
“Just as, monks, on the Himalayan mountains there is a species of bird called the karavīka, which has a sweet voice, a melodious voice, a pleasant voice, and a lovely voice;
even so, monks, Prince Vipassī had a sweet voice, a melodious voice, a pleasant voice, and a lovely voice.
Furthermore, monks, as soon as Prince Vipassī was born, the divine eye born of karmic fruition appeared to him, by means of which he could see for a league all around, both by day and by night.”
“Monks, as soon as Prince Vipassī was born, he gazed with unblinking eyes, just like the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
‘The prince gazes with unblinking eyes,’ monks, so the designation ‘Vipassī, Vipassī’ arose for Prince Vipassī.
Then, monks, King Bandhuma, while seated in the court of justice, had Prince Vipassī sit on his lap and instructed him in state affairs.”
Thereupon, monks, while sitting on his father’s lap, Prince Vipassī would consider things thoroughly and determine their meaning according to the right method.
Because the prince considered things thoroughly and determined their meaning according to the right method, monks, the designation “Vipassī, Vipassī” arose for him even more so.
Then, monks, King Bandhumā had three palaces built for Prince Vipassī: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer.
He provided the five strands of sensual pleasure.
There, monks, Prince Vipassī, while being entertained by female musicians in the summer palace for four months, did not descend from the upper palace.
This concludes the first recitation section.
5. The Old Man.
Then, monks, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, Prince Vipassī addressed his charioteer:
“Yoke, my dear charioteer, the finest carriages; let us go to the pleasure grove to see the beautiful countryside.”
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the charioteer replied to Prince Vipassī. Having harnessed various magnificent vehicles, he informed Prince Vipassī:
‘Your Majesty, the various magnificent vehicles are ready;
now is the time for you to do as you deem fit.’
Then, monks, Prince Vipassī, having mounted a fine carriage and proceeding in a procession of fine carriages, went out to the pleasure grounds.

As he was going to the pleasure grounds, monks, Prince Vipassī saw a man who was aged, bent like a roof-rafter, decrepit, leaning on a staff for support, trembling as he walked, afflicted, and past his youth.
Having seen him, he addressed the charioteer:
“But, dear charioteer, what has this man done?
His hair is not like that of others, and his body is not like that of others.
“This man, sire, is called ‘old’.”
“But what is this, dear charioteer, that is called ‘old’?
“Sire, this is what is called ‘old. He will not have long to live now.
“But what, dear charioteer, am I also subject to old age, not exempt from old age?”
“‘And you, O King, and we—all of us are subject to old age; none of us have transcended old age.
‘In that case, my dear charioteer, enough of going to the park today. Turn back from here toward the inner palace.
‘Very well, Your Majesty,’ the charioteer replied to Prince Vipassī, and he turned back from there toward the inner palace.”
Thereupon, monks, Prince Vipassī, having gone to the inner palace, sat brooding, pained and dejected:
"Alas, indeed, is this thing called birth! For when one is born, aging is bound to appear.
Then, monks, King Bandhuma summoned his charioteer and said this to him:
‘Well, dear charioteer, did the prince enjoy the park grounds? Was the prince pleased with the park grounds, dear charioteer?
‘Indeed, Your Majesty, the prince did not enjoy the park grounds; indeed, Your Majesty, the prince was not pleased with the park grounds.
‘But what, dear charioteer, did the prince see as he was being driven to the park grounds?’

“Your Majesty, as the prince was being driven out to the park, he saw a man who was aged, bent like a roof-rafter, hunched, leaning on a staff for support, trembling as he walked, afflicted, and past his youth.
Having seen him, he said this to me:
‘But, my dear charioteer, what has been done to this man? His hair is not like that of others, and his body is not like that of others.’”
“That, Your Majesty, is what is called ‘old’.
“But what, my dear charioteer, is this that is called ‘old’?
“That, Your Majesty, is what is called ‘old’; he will not have long more to live.”
“But what, my dear charioteer, am I also subject to old age, not exempt from old age?
“Your majesty and we all are subject to old age, not exempt from old age.
“In that case, my dear charioteer, enough of the pleasure park for today; turn back from here toward the inner palace.”
“Yes, Your Majesty,” I replied to Prince Vipassī, and I departed from the inner palace.
Once the prince had gone to the inner palace, he sat brooding, distressed and dejected:
“Alas, indeed, is this so-called birth! For where there is birth, aging is seen for one who has been born.”
6. The Sick Man.
Then, monks, it occurred to King Bandhuma:

“May it not be that Prince Vipassī does not exercise sovereignty; may it not be that Prince Vipassī goes forth from the home life into homelessness; may it not be that the words of the brahmins who read omens prove true!”
Then, monks, King Bandhuma provided Prince Vipassī with even more of the five strands of sensual pleasure, thinking:
‘May Prince Vipassī rule the kingdom; may Prince Vipassī not go forth from the home life into homelessness; may the words of the Brahmins who made the prediction prove false.
Thereupon, monks, Prince Vipassī enjoyed himself, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Then, monks, after many years had passed for Prince Vipassī...
Prince Vipassī, while being driven out to the park, saw a man who was afflicted, suffering, gravely ill,
lying fouled in his own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some and laid down by others.
Having seen him, he addressed the charioteer:
“But what has this man done, dear charioteer?
His eyes are not like those of others, and his body is not like that of others.”
‘That, Your Majesty, is what is called “one who is afflicted with disease.
‘But why, my dear charioteer, is he called “one who is afflicted with disease”?
‘He is called “one who is afflicted with disease,” Your Majesty, because perhaps he might recover from that ailment.’
"But, dear charioteer, am I also subject to illness, not exempt from illness?
"Your Majesty, both you and we are all subject to illness; none of us are exempt from illness.
"In that case, dear charioteer, enough of the pleasure park for today. Turn back from here toward the inner palace."
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the charioteer replied to Prince Vipassī, and he drove back from there to the inner palace.
There, monks, having returned to the inner palace, Prince Vipassī brooded, distressed and dejected:
“Alas! This thing called birth is truly wretched, for when one has been born, aging is seen, and sickness is seen.”
Then, monks, King Bandhumā, having summoned his charioteer, said this to him:
“I hope, dear charioteer, that the prince enjoyed himself in the park; I hope, dear charioteer, that the prince was pleased with the park grounds?
“Indeed, Your Majesty, the prince did not enjoy himself in the park; indeed, Your Majesty, the prince was not pleased with the park grounds.”
"But what did the prince see, good charioteer, as he was being driven out to the pleasure grove?

"Your Majesty, as the prince was being driven out to the pleasure grove, he saw a man who was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, lying fouled in his own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some and laid down by others.
Having seen him, he said this to me:"
“But, dear charioteer, what has this man done that his eyes are not like those of others and his body is not like that of others?
“Sire, he is called ‘one who is afflicted with disease.
“But what does it mean, dear charioteer, to be ‘afflicted with disease’?”
“Sire, this man is called ‘sick’; perhaps he might even recover from that affliction.
“But what, my dear charioteer, am I too subject to sickness, not exempt from sickness?
“Both you, sire, and we all are subject to sickness, not exempt from sickness.”
“Therefore, dear charioteer, enough of going to the park today; turn back from here toward the inner palace.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” I replied to Prince Vipassī, and I turned back from there toward the inner palace.
Then, Your Majesty, having gone to the inner palace, the prince sat brooding, distressed and dejected:

“Alas, sirs, let there be an end to this thing called birth, for where there is birth, aging is seen, and sickness is seen. Then, monks, it occurred to King Bandhumā: “Alas, sirs, let there be an end to this thing called birth, for where there is birth, aging is seen, and sickness is seen. Then, monks, King Bandhumā thought: “It would be well if I were to go forth from the household life into homelessness while I am still young, possessed of black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, before I have experienced old age. Then, monks, King Bandhumā went to his barber and said: “If you see, barber, that my head is grey-haired, report to me.”—“Yes, sire,” the barber replied to King Bandhumā. Some time later, as King Bandhumā was seated on the upper terrace of his palace enjoying the view, the barber saw grey hairs on the king’s head and reported this to him: “Sire, grey hairs are seen on your head.”—“Pull them out, barber, and place them in my hand.”—“Yes, sire,” the barber replied to King Bandhumā. Having pulled them out, he placed them in the king’s hand. Then, monks, King Bandhumā took those grey hairs in his hand and addressed his retinue:

“Behold, sirs, these grey hairs. Grey hairs, sirs, have appeared in me. I am now old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life. I too am subject to aging; I cannot escape it. It would be well, sirs, if I were to go forth from the household life into homelessness while I am still young, possessed of black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, before I have experienced old age. Then, monks, King Bandhumā addressed his chief minister: “I wish, chief minister, to go forth from the household life into homelessness while I am still young, possessed of black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, before I have experienced old age. Therefore, chief minister, whatever kings there are who are my equals or superior, report this to them: ‘King Bandhumā, sirs, wishes to go forth from the household life into homelessness while he is still young, possessed of black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, before he has experienced old age. If you, sirs, desire to go forth from the household life into homelessness, come along with King Bandhumā. —“Yes, sire,” the chief minister replied to King Bandhumā. Then, monks, King Bandhumā addressed his charioteer: “I wish, charioteer, to go forth from the household life into homelessness while I am still young, possessed of black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, before I have experienced old age. Therefore, charioteer, harness a swift chariot and bring it here. I shall mount it and depart.”—“Yes, sire,” the charioteer replied to King Bandhumā. Then, monks, King Bandhumā mounted the swift chariot and departed from Sāketa toward Benares. On the way, he saw a man who was decrepit, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, supported by a staff, trembling and leaning on it, bent over, with a hunched back, going along by means of a support. Seeing him, he asked his charioteer: “What kind of man, charioteer, is this?”—“Sire, this is a man who is decrepit, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, supported by a staff, trembling and leaning on it, bent over, with a hunched back, going along by means of a support.”—“Why is he called ‘decrepit’?”—“Sire, his teeth have fallen out, his hair has turned white, his body is wrinkled, his limbs are bent, he is coughing and wheezing, his youth has passed, his lifespan is spent, and he is decrepit. Therefore, sire, he is called ‘decrepit.’”—“Charioteer, turn the chariot around at this very spot. I do not wish to go further. I am subject to this condition; I cannot escape it.”—“Yes, sire,” the charioteer replied to King Bandhumā. Then, monks, King Bandhumā descended from the swift chariot at that very spot and sat down on a prepared seat. Sitting there, he addressed his charioteer: “What kind of man, charioteer, is this?”—“Sire, this is a man who is decrepit, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, supported by a staff, trembling and leaning on it, bent over, with a hunched back, going along by means of a support.”—“Why is he called ‘decrepit’?”—“Sire, his teeth have fallen out, his hair has turned white, his body is wrinkled, his limbs are bent, he is coughing and wheezing, his youth has passed, his lifespan is spent, and he is decrepit. Therefore, sire, he is called ‘decrepit.’”—“Charioteer, turn the chariot around at this very spot. I do not wish to go further. “‘That one, Your Majesty, is called a renunciant.

“I am indeed called a renunciant, O King: it is good to practice the Dhamma, good to practice equanimity, good to perform wholesome deeds, good to perform meritorious deeds, good is non-violence, and good is compassion for living beings.”

11. The Bodhisatta’s Resolve Then, monks, as the Bodhisatta Vipassī had retired to his dwelling, gone into seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble! It is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn; yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death.
When, indeed, will an escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be made known?
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? With what as condition does aging-and-death arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does birth come to be? With what as condition does birth arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is existence, birth comes to be; with existence as condition, birth arises.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does existence come to be? With what as condition does existence arise?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisattva Vipassī a realization by means of wisdom:
"When there is clinging, existence comes to be; with clinging as condition, there is existence.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisattva Vipassī:
‘When what exists does clinging come to be? With what as condition does clinging arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When craving exists, clinging comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does craving come to be? With what as condition does craving arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there came to the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is feeling, craving comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving arises.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does feeling come to be? With what as condition does feeling arise?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When there is contact, feeling comes to be; feeling has contact as its condition.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does contact come to be? By what condition does contact arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassi an awakening through wisdom:
‘When the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does the sixfold sense base come to be? With what as condition does the sixfold sense base arise?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there came to the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom.
‘When there is name-and-form, the six sense bases come to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does name-and-form come to be? By what condition does name-and-form arise?’
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does consciousness come to be? With what as condition does consciousness arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassi a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When name-and-form exists, consciousness comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"This consciousness turns back from name-and-form; it does not go further than this.
It is to this extent that one is born, or ages, or dies, or passes away, or reappears—that is to say,"

With name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises;

with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
"Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
"Origin, origin," monks, regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist do aging and death not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of aging and death?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When birth does not exist, aging and death do not come to be; through the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisattva Vipassī:
"In the absence of what does birth not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of birth?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisattva Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is no becoming, birth does not come to be; with the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘Now, when what is absent does becoming not come to be? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of becoming?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When clinging does not exist, becoming does not come to be; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what is absent does grasping not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of grasping occur?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī an awakening through wisdom:
‘When craving is absent, grasping does not come to be; through the cessation of craving, grasping ceases.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"In the absence of what does craving not come to be? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of craving?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is no feeling, craving does not arise; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘In the absence of what does feeling not arise? With the cessation of what does feeling cease?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
"When contact does not exist, feeling does not arise; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist does contact not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of contact occur?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When the six sense bases do not exist, contact does not come to be; with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"In what being absent does the sixfold sense base not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the sixfold sense base cease?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases do not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘In the absence of what does name-and-form not come to be? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of name-and-form?’”
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When consciousness does not exist, name-and-form does not come to be; with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist does consciousness not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness occur?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘This path has been discovered by me for full enlightenment, namely:

with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases.’
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
"Cessation, cessation," monks, regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.
Then, monks, after some time, the Bodhisatta Vipassī dwelt contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging.
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is perception, such its origin, such its passing away.’
‘Such are volitional formations, such their origin, such their passing away;
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.

Then, monks, it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:

Then, monks, it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:

This generation, indeed, delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
For this generation that delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this point is difficult to see: namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination.

‘If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be wearying for me, that would be troublesome.

And then, monks, these marvelous verses, never heard before, occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: “By hardship was it attained by me, and it is profound, subtle, and hard to see. But those who are blinded by passion will not perceive it;
it is enough for me to be weary.”
Enough now with explaining;
this Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those overcome by lust and hatred.
Those who are stained by passion will not see that which goes against the stream, which is subtle, profound, hard to see, and minute.
"Enveloped by the mass of ignorance.
Thus, monks, as the Blessed One Vipassī—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—reflected, his mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.
Then, monks, a certain Great Brahmā, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—thought this:

"Alas, sirs, the world is perishing! Alas, sirs, the world is being destroyed! For the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dhamma.
Then, monks, that Great Brahmā, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One Vipassī.
He appeared before the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, monks,
that Great Brahmā arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
He said this to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma; let the Sugata teach the Dhamma.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma.”
‘There will be those who understand the Dhamma.
When this was said, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, said this to that Great Brahmā:
‘Brahmā, it occurred to me too:’
“What if I were to teach the Dhamma?

“This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.”
But this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, rejoices in attachment.
