This state, too, is difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
“If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be weariness for me, that would be vexation for me.

And then, Brahmā, these marvelous verses, never heard before, occurred to me: “Attained by me with difficulty, it would be a weariness for me to teach it; for those who do not know, it is hard to make them understand.”
Enough now with explaining;
this Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those overcome by lust and hatred.
Those who are stained by passion will not see that which goes against the stream, which is subtle, profound, hard to see, and minute.
“Enveloped by the mass of ignorance.
Thus, Brahmā, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.
A second time also, monks, that Great Brahmā... [as before]...’"
And for a third time, monks, that Great Brahmā said this to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:

“May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma! There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; there will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
Then, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having understood Brahmā’s entreaty and out of compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye.
Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good disposition and of bad disposition.

Some were easy to instruct and some difficult to instruct; some lived perceiving the danger in the world beyond and in moral transgression, while others lived without perceiving the danger in the world beyond and in moral transgression.
Just as in a bed of blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses, some of the lotuses...
Or there are water-born blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, not rising above the water, nourished while submerged within it.
Or some of those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, stand level with the water. Or some of those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses...
Born in water, grown up in water, yet standing out above the water and unsullied by it—
just so, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye,
saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions...

Some were easy to instruct and some difficult to instruct; some dwelt seeing fear in the world beyond and in moral transgression, while others dwelt not seeing fear in the world beyond and in moral transgression.

Then, monks, that Great Brahmā, having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in verses:
"Just as one standing on the summit of a mountain might see the people all around, even so,
O wise one, does one who consists of the Dhamma [see] in this same way."
Having ascended the palace, O All-Seeing One,
free from sorrow, look down upon the people overwhelmed by grief,
who are overcome by birth and old age.
Arise, O hero, victor in battle!
O caravan-leader free from debt, wander through the world;
teach the Dhamma, O Blessed One.
‘They shall become knowers.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed that Great Brahmā with a verse:
‘The doors to the Deathless have been opened for them;’
"Let those who have ears release their faith!
O Brahmā, perceiving that it would cause harm,
I did not speak the sublime Dhamma among men."
Then, monks, that Great Brahmā, thinking: "I have been granted leave by the Blessed One Vipassī,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the teaching of the Dhamma," paid homage to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
kept him on his right, and vanished right there.
13. The Pair of Chief Disciples.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?”
‘Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?
Then, monks, it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:

‘These two, Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa the son of the chaplain, reside in the royal capital of Bandhumatī; they are wise, competent, and intelligent, and for a long time they have been of little dust in their eyes.’
"What if I were now to teach the Dhamma first to Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest? They will quickly understand this Dhamma.

Then, monks, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so did the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, vanish from the foot of the Bodhi tree... [and appear before them].
Having vanished from there, he reappeared in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, at the Khema Deer Park.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the park keeper:
“Come, my good park keeper, enter the royal capital of Bandhumatī and say this to Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest:”
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī and is staying in the Khema Deer Park;
he desires to see you. “Very well, venerable sir,” the park keeper replied to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having entered the royal capital of Bandhumatī, he said this to Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest:
“Vipassī, bhante, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī and is staying in the Khema Deer Park;

he wishes to see you. Then, monks, Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest, had various fine carriages prepared, mounted each upon a fine carriage, and [departed] from Bandhumatī with their respective fine carriages.
They set out from the capital city. They proceeded toward Khema Migadāya.

Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would permit for a vehicle, they alighted from their carriages and approached the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, on foot.
Having approached, [they went to] the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant...
Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, they sat down to one side.
To them, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, delivered a progressive discourse;
that is to say, he spoke on generosity, on virtue, and on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that his mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then set forth the Dhamma teaching peculiar to Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains, would perfectly absorb a dye;
In the same way, in that very seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose for both Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the chaplain:
"Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.

Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma, they crossed over doubt, were freed from perplexity, and became independent of others in the Teacher's Dispensation.
Having attained fearlessness and being independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, they said this to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or as one might show the way to one who has lost their path, or as one might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with sight may see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
We go for refuge, Bhante, to the Blessed One and to the Dhamma.
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full ordination.

And so, monks, Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest, received the going-forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
He proclaimed the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of volitional formations, and the benefit in Nibbāna.
As they were being instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One Vipassi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with this discourse on the Dhamma,
before long their minds were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
14. The Great Multitude’s Going-forth.
Monks, a great multitude of eighty-four thousand people in the royal capital of Bandhumatī heard:
“The Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, it is said, has arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī and is staying in the Khema Deer Park.”

“Khaṇḍa, it seems, the prince, and Tissa, the son of the family priest, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having heard this, it occurred to them:
“Surely this Dhamma and Discipline is no trivial matter, nor is this going forth a trivial thing, since Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest,
have shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron robes,
and gone forth from the home life into homelessness.”

“Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the son of the family priest, will shave off their hair and beards, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness— how much more so should we? Then, monks,

that great multitude of eighty-four thousand people departed from the royal capital of Bandhumatī and went to Khema’s Deer Park, where the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was staying.
Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and sat down to one side.
To them, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, delivered a graduated discourse. That is to say:

he expounded upon the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue, and the discourse on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that his mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and serene, he then set forth that Dhamma exposition which is uniquely supreme among the Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would perfectly absorb a dye;
In the same way, in those very seats, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose for those eighty-four thousand beings:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.
Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma, they crossed over doubt, became free from perplexity, and were no longer dependent on others.
Having attained fearlessness and being independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or as one might show the way to one who has lost his path, or as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with sight may see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
We go for refuge, Bhante, to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full ordination.
Bhikkhus, those eighty-four thousand beings received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; they received the full ordination.
Then the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
He proclaimed the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of volitional formations, and the benefit in Nibbāna.
As they were being instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with this discourse on the Dhamma,
before long their minds were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
15. The Realization of the Dhamma by Those Who Went Forth First.
Bhikkhus, those eighty-four thousand who had gone forth previously heard:

“It is said that the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī and is staying in the Khema Deer Park, and it is said that he teaches the Dhamma.”
Then, monks, those eighty-four thousand who had gone forth approached the royal capital of Bandhumatī,
the Khema Deer Park, and the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having approached,
they paid homage to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and sat down to one side.
To them the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, gave a gradual discourse. That is to say:
he spoke on generosity, on virtue, and on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that their minds were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he revealed that which is the special Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye, even so, to those eighty-four thousand who had gone forth, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in that very seat: [that all things subject to origination are subject to cessation].
‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.
Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;

having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence, and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One.]”
"In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma in many ways.
Venerable sir, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir; may we receive full ordination."
Bhikkhus, those eighty-four thousand who had gone forth received the going-forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma;
he proclaimed the danger, degradation, and defilement of conditioned phenomena, and the blessing of Nibbāna.

As they were being instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with a discourse on the Dhamma, before long their minds were liberated from the taints through non-clinging. 16.
Permission to Wander Forth.
Now at that time, monks, a great community of bhikkhus—six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus—was residing in the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Then, monks, while the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:

"At present, there is a great community of bhikkhus residing in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, numbering six million eight hundred thousand. What if I were to give permission to the bhikkhus: [to go wandering]?"
“Wander forth, bhikkhus, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Let not two of you go by one way.
Teach, bhikkhus, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure.”
“There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are declining;
there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
However, after the lapse of six years, the royal capital Bandhumatī must be approached for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.”
Then, monks, a certain Great Brahmā, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One Vipassī.
He appeared before the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, monks,
that Great Brahmā arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One Vipassī,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and said this to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
Now, Bhante, the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus dwells here in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, numbering six million eight hundred thousand. May the Blessed One grant permission to the bhikkhus:
‘Go forth, bhikkhus, on tour for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.’”
"Do not go two by one.
Teach, monks, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; proclaim the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are falling away; there will be those who understand the Dhamma."
"Moreover, venerable sir, we shall act in such a way that at the end of each six years the bhikkhus will approach the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
This, monks, is what that Great Brahmā said.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and keeping him to his right, he vanished right there.
Then, monks, in the evening, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having emerged from seclusion, addressed the monks:
“Monks, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘At present, there is a great community of monks residing here in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, numbering six million eight hundred thousand.’”
What if I were now to authorize the monks:
"Go forth, monks, on tour for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans;
let not two of you go by one way."
“Proclaim, monks, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; reveal the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; they will become knowers of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, at the end of six years, the royal capital of Bandhumatī must be visited for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.”
Then, monks, a certain Great Brahmā, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in my mind,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before me.
Then, monks, that Great Brahmā, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward me and said this to me:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
At present, venerable sir, a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus is residing at the royal capital of Bandhumatī, numbering six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One give permission to the bhikkhus:
‘Go forth, bhikkhus, on tour for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans;
let not two go by one way.’”
"Proclaim the Dhamma, bhikkhus...
there are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; they will become knowers of the Dhamma.
"Very well, venerable sir, we shall act in such a way that at the end of each six years the bhikkhus will approach the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the recitation of the Pātimokkha."
"Monks, that Great Brahmā said this.
Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me with his right side toward me, and vanished right there.

'I authorize you, monks, to go on a wandering tour for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.'"
Do not go two by one;

teach, monks, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, and proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma.
"There will be those who understand the Dhamma.
Moreover, monks, at the end of each six years, you must go to the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Then, monks, the monks set out on their travels through the countryside almost entirely on the very same day.
Now at that time, there were eighty-four thousand monasteries in Jambudīpa.
When one year had passed, the deities raised their voices, crying out:
“One year, friends, has now passed!”
"Now five years remain;
at the end of five years, the royal capital of Bandhumatī must be approached for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
When two years had passed...
When three years had passed… when four years had passed… when five years had passed,
the deities raised their voices, crying out:
“Venerable sirs, five years have indeed passed;
now only one year remains.
At the end of that one year, we must go to the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.”
When six years had passed, the deities raised their voices, saying:
"Friends, six years have indeed passed;
it is now the time to approach the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the recitation of the Pātimokkha."

Then, monks, some of those monks by means of their own psychic power and some by means of the psychic power of the deities arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī in a single day for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
There, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, recited the Pātimokkha to the Saṅgha of monks thus:
“Patience is the supreme austerity; forbearance is the highest.”
The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme;
for one who harms others has not gone forth,
nor is one a recluse who oppresses others.
To refrain from all evil,
to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one's own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
This is the teaching of the Buddhas:
non-reproach, non-violence,
and restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
Moderation in food,
a secluded dwelling,
and application to the higher mind—
“This is the teaching of the Buddhas. 17.
The Declaration of a Deity “Bhikkhus, on one occasion I was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a royal sāla tree.”
“Bhikkhus, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘There is no abode of beings that has not been visited by me during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa deities.
What if I were now to approach the Suddhāvāsa deities?’”
Then, monks, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so, having vanished from the Sāla-tree king at Ukkatthā in the Subhaga Grove,
I reappeared among the Aviha devas.
In that assembly of devas, bhikkhus, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas, approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, bhikkhus, those devas said this to me:
“Ninety-one aeons ago, friends, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
Friends, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of kṣatriya birth; he arose in a kṣatriya family.
Friends, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan.”
"Venerable sirs, the lifespan of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī, was eighty thousand years.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Pāṭali tree.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī had a pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa, who were a supreme and auspicious pair."
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had three assemblies of disciples.
One assembly of disciples consisted of sixty-eight hundred thousand bhikkhus;
one assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand bhikkhus; and one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had these three assemblies of disciples,
all of whom were destroyers of the taints.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a bhikkhu named Asoka as his attendant, his chief attendant.
Vipassī, sirs, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a father named King Bandhumā.
His mother, the queen who bore him, was named Bandhumatī.
For King Bandhumā, there was a royal capital city named Bandhumatī.

“Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had such an going-forth, such an ordination, such an exertion, such an awakening, and such a turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī and having dispelled sensual desire for sense-pleasures, we have been reborn here. … [as before] …
In that very assembly of devas, bhikkhus, many thousands and many hundreds of thousands of devas approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, bhikkhus, those devas said this to me:
"In this very auspicious aeon, friends, the Blessed One has now arisen in the world as an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Blessed One, friends, is a kshatriya by birth, born into a kshatriya family.
The Blessed One, friends, belongs to the Gotama clan."
"Venerable sirs, the lifespan of the Blessed One was short, limited, and brief; whoever lives long does so for at most a hundred years or slightly more.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One attained full enlightenment at the foot of an Assattha tree.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One had a pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the foremost and auspicious pair."

Venerable sirs, the Blessed One had one assembly of disciples consisting of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. Venerable sirs, this was the one assembly of the Blessed One’s disciples, all of whom were indeed those whose taints were exhausted.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One’s attendant was the bhikkhu named Ānanda, his chief personal attendant.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One’s father was the king named Suddhodana.
The queen named Māyā was his mother, his progenitress.
The city named Kapilavatthu was the royal capital.
Venerable sirs, such was the Blessed One’s great departure; such was his renunciation; such was his striving; such was his full awakening; such was his setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
“‘It is because we, dear sirs, having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One and having removed sensual desire for sense pleasures, have been reborn here.
Then, monks, together with the Aviha devas, I approached the Atappa devas...
Then, monks, together with the Aviha devas and the Atappa devas, I approached the Sudassa devas.”
Then, monks, together with the Aviha devas, the Atappa devas, and the Sudassa devas,
I approached the Sudassi devas. Then, monks, together with the Aviha devas,
the Atappa devas, the Sudassa devas, and the Sudassi devas, I approached the Akaniṭṭha devas.
I approached that assembly of devas. There, monks, many thousands and many hundreds of thousands of devas approached me, and having approached and paid homage to me, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, monks, those devas said this to me:
“Ninety-one aeons ago, friends, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
Friends, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of kṣatriya birth;
he arose in a kṣatriya family.”
Vipassī, friends, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan.
The lifespan of Vipassī, friends, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years.
Vipassī, friends, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Pāṭali tree.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa, who were a most auspicious pair.
Venerable sirs, there were three assemblies of disciples for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
One assembly of disciples consisted of six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.
There was one assembly of disciples consisting of one hundred thousand bhikkhus;
there was another assembly of disciples consisting of eighty thousand bhikkhus.
These, friends, were the three assemblies of disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—all of whom had destroyed the taints.
Vipassi, friends, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a bhikkhu named Asoka who was his attendant, his chief attendant.
Vipassi, friends, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a father named King Bandhuma and a mother named Queen Bandhumatī, who gave him birth.
For King Bandhuma, the royal capital was the city named Bandhumatī.

“Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī—the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—had such a going-forth, such an ordination, such an exertion, such an awakening, and such a turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Having practiced the holy life under that Blessed One Vipassī and having dispelled sensual desire for sense pleasures, we have been reborn here.
In that very assembly of devas, O bhikkhus, there were many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas.
They approached me; having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those deities said this to me:
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, O venerable sirs, there appeared the Blessed One Sikhī... [and so on] ...”
"Venerable sirs, we [served] under the Blessed One Sikhī; indeed, venerable sirs, in that very thirty-first aeon, we [served] under the Blessed One Vessabhū...
Venerable sirs, we [served] under the Blessed One Vessabhū...
Indeed, venerable sirs, in this very Bhaddakappa aeon, we [served] under the Blessed Ones Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa..."
‘We, dear sir, having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One Kakusandha, under Koṇāgamana, and under Kassapa, and having abandoned sensual desire for sense pleasures, have been reborn here.
Then, monks, many thousands of deities, many hundreds of thousands of deities from that very host of gods, approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, they stood to one side. Standing to one side...
"Standing there, bhikkhus, those deities said this to me:
'In this very auspicious aeon, dear sir, the Blessed One has now arisen in the world as an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
The Blessed One, dear sir, is a khattiya by birth; he has arisen in a khattiya family.'"
"Venerable sirs, the Blessed One Gotama is [known] by his clan.
Venerable sirs, the lifespan of the Blessed One is short, limited, and brief; whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One attained full enlightenment at the foot of an Assattha tree."
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One had a pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna, an excellent pair.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One had one assembly of disciples consisting of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.
Venerable sirs, this was the one assembly of the Blessed One’s disciples, all of whom were indeed those whose taints were destroyed.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One’s attendant, his chief personal attendant, was the bhikkhu named Ānanda.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One’s father was King Suddhodana;
Queen Māyā was his mother, who gave him birth.
“There was a city named Kapilavatthu that served as the royal capital.
Venerable sirs, such was the Blessed One’s great departure; such was his renunciation; such was his striving; such was his full awakening; and such was his turning of the wheel of Dhamma.
Having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One and having dispelled sensual desire for sense pleasures, we have been reborn here.”
Thus, monks, this very element of Dhamma has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata; because this element of Dhamma has been thoroughly penetrated,
the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the faring-on has been cut off, the course has been ended, the round has been exhausted,
and who have passed beyond all suffering— recollecting them by their birth, by their names, and by their clans.
He recollects even the measure of their lifespans; he recollects even their pairs of disciples; he recollects even their assemblies of disciples, thinking:
"Those Blessed Ones were of such birth"; and also:
"Those Blessed Ones were of such names, such clans, such conduct, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such dwellings, and such liberation."
The deities also informed the Tathāgata of this matter, whereby the Tathāgata remembers the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna,
for whom the proliferation of conceptualization has been cut off, the cycle of rebirth has been severed, the round of existence has been brought to an end,
and who have transcended all suffering— remembering them by their birth, by their names, by their clans, by the measure of their lifespans, and even by their pairs of chief disciples.
He recollects them, and he also recollects the assemblies of disciples: “Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth,” and also:
“Those Blessed Ones were of such names, such clans, such virtue, such Dhamma, such wisdom, such a way of abiding, and such liberation.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Mahāpadāna Sutta, the first, is finished.
